introduction: Two statements stand together in these readings. Revelation does not end: the sovereignty of God has no end, and other Manifestations will come. Yet no one may claim a revelation before a full thousand years have passed from Bahá’u’lláh's own, the years to be counted plainly; and the cycle he opens is said to run for hundreds of thousands of years. Other scriptures have their own words of expectation and of closure, a prophet like Moses, another Comforter, the Seal of the Prophets, the faith once delivered, and their own warnings about false claimants, and these are set beside the readings. Peter's thousand years that are as a day, the test of fruits, and Tennyson and Emerson on forms that outlast their life are given as contrasts.
questions: What do the readings leave open about the future, and what do they close?
Every tradition quoted here expects more to come and also guards what it has received. How do the readings' thousand years compare with the Seal of the Prophets, or the faith once delivered?

Jesus says prophets are known by their fruits; the readings say a claimant within the thousand years is false whatever signs he brings. How would you explain the rule to someone who thinks fruits should decide?
Bahá’u’lláh says he fears for the one who will come after him. What does that ask of his own followers?
Tennyson fears that one good custom may corrupt the world. What keeps a long dispensation alive?

outside.why: Jesus warns of false Christs and false prophets who will show great signs and wonders.
Deuteronomy tests one who speaks in God's name by whether the thing comes to pass. How does a test by date relate to a test by outcome?
Paul tells the Galatians to reject any other gospel, though an angel from heaven should preach it.
John's letter tells believers to try the spirits, because many false prophets are gone out.
The Qur’an calls Muhammad the Seal of the Prophets, a verse most Muslims read as closing prophecy. How does a faith that arose after it understand its own thousand-year rule?
The psalm says a thousand years in God's sight are but as yesterday when it is past.
Peter says that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. Why do the readings insist that these years need no interpretation?
Jesus says that of that day and hour knoweth no man, but the Father only.
Krishna says that at the close of each kalpa all things return to him, and at its beginning issue forth again.
Jesus says that new wine is put into new bottles, and both are preserved.
Jesus promises another Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who shall abide with his followers for ever.
Jesus laments the city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to it.
Jesus says he has yet many things to say, which his hearers cannot bear now.
Isaiah has God say: behold, I will do a new thing; shall ye not know it?
The Qur’an says that for everything there is a time prescribed, and no messenger brings a sign unbidden.
The Preacher says there is a season and a time to every purpose under heaven.
Jesus warns of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.
Gamaliel advised leaving a new claim alone: if it be of men it will come to nought. Is his counsel a safer guide than a rule, or a weaker one?
Jesus says that prophets are known by their fruits. Can a rule of time rightly outweigh every sign and every fruit?
Jude exhorts believers to contend for the faith once delivered unto the saints.
Mill warns that a truth not fully and fearlessly discussed is held as a dead dogma. How does a word called final stay a living one over a thousand years?
Hebrews says God spoke at sundry times and in divers manners, and in these last days by his Son.
Muhammad is told to say that he is no new thing among the messengers.
The Lord of John's vision says: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending.
Moses tells Israel that God will raise up a prophet like unto him, and unto him they shall hearken.
Malachi has God promise a messenger to come: behold, I will send my messenger before me.
John sees the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven.
The Song of Songs says: the winter is past, the flowers appear on the earth.
Shelley asks the wind to be a trumpet of prophecy: if winter comes, can spring be far behind?
At the seventh trumpet voices declare that the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord.
Isaiah has God create new heavens and a new earth, and the former shall not be remembered.
The psalm says: thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion endures throughout all generations.
The Qur’an says that a day with God is as a thousand years of what ye reckon.
The Qur’an speaks of a day whereof the span is fifty thousand years.
Daniel is told to seal the book till the time of the end, when knowledge shall be increased.
Tennyson ends on one far-off divine event to which the whole creation moves.
Habakkuk is told that the vision is for an appointed time: though it tarry, wait for it.
Peter speaks of times of refreshing to come from the presence of the Lord.
Isaiah asks to whom God can be likened, or what likeness compared to him.
Origen asks who of understanding will suppose that a first, second and third day existed without a sun.
Jesus says: walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you.
In John's vision the Lord stands at the door and knocks, waiting for whoever will open.
The Qur’an says that for every nation there is a messenger, a promise older than any one faith.
Krishna says that when righteousness declines he comes forth, age after age.
Maimonides holds that one should not presume the Messianic king must work miracles and wonders.
The Preacher says the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
Jesus asks: when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?
Yeats, seeing the best lack all conviction, says: surely some revelation is at hand.
Jesus says that because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
Lamentations says that the Lord's mercies are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
The Preacher says the sun also ariseth, and goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose.
Rumi says the lamps are different, but the Light is the same.
Jesus says the earth brings forth first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn.
Paul says: when I was a child I understood as a child, but when I became a man I put away childish things.
Micah foresees nations learning war no more, and every man under his vine and fig tree.
The psalmist says such knowledge is too wonderful for him: it is high, he cannot attain unto it.
The psalmist asks to be taught to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Paul says the letter kills, but the spirit gives life, his rule for reading a text.
Tennyson says the old order changes, lest one good custom should corrupt the world. What keeps a dispensation of a thousand years or more from that?
John says: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
Jesus speaks of those who honour dead prophets and say they would not have joined in shedding their blood.

Emerson asks why we should not also enjoy an original relation to the universe, and not see through the eyes of the fathers. What does a long interval between revelations ask of the generations within it?

luke-shall-he-find-faith.text: Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth
